citation.title: Does the Correspondence Bias Apply to Social Robots?: Dispositional and Situational Attributions of Human Versus Robot Behavior

reading.source_scope_note: Randomized2×2×2online video experiment on human judgments of a human or Pepper speech.267recruited,231retained after checks and exclusion of legalization opponents. It measures attributed attitudes, confidence and global impressions. Correspondence inference is not by itself a proven error, mental state, blame judgment or calibrated-confidence result. FFAB is defined in background, not directly tested by varying robot form.

study.sample: 267USMTurk adults paid$2;231retained after audio/topic checks and excluding opponents of medical-marijuana legalization. Mean age43.32SD11.36, range24–71;118male,110female,2prefer not answer,1genderfluid;79%White,60%bachelor degree or higher.36exclusions have no reason×condition flow. Opponents are excluded to operationalize popularity, limiting generalization.
study.design: Randomized2agent(human/Pepper)×2stance(pro/anti legalization)×2choice(chosen/assigned)between-subject video design. One-minute parallel speeches, a single human graduate assistant and a single Pepper robot. Speech rate and gestures described as comparable; identity, voice and appearance remain bundled. Mood measured before exposure and statistically controlled, not randomized.
study.postselection: Participants’ own topic attitudes are measured after the video and used for exclusion. If exposure affected those attitudes, conditioning on them could affect randomized comparability. This risk is not proof it occurred; no preregistration or condition-specific exclusion data establish the effect.
study.outcomes: Seven-point attributed true attitude, single confidence judgment, and eight bipolar global-impression items. Impressions form one reported component, eigenvalue5.27,65.86%variance,α.92. Two mood itemsr.92yieldα.96, internally coherent. Summed scores are reported on an item-mean1–7scale; constant rescaling would not by itself invalidate Ftests.
study.attitude_results: SourcebehaviorF1,220=152.98,η².41; agentF1,220=7.39,η².03; formalagent×behaviorF1,220=16.15, p<.001,η².07. Attitudes follow expressed stance more strongly for Pepper, especially unpopular speech. This actual interaction supports a differential pattern, not merely significant-versus-nonsignificant subgroup comparisons.

study.conceptual_scope: Source explicitly separates broader FAE(overweighting disposition/underweighting situation)from narrower behavior-congruent disposition inference. Actual true attitudes are unknown and the meaning of robot attitude is contested; correspondence does not by itself establish an error or uniquely identify a causal theory.
study.s_theory: Lack of situational theory, failed application, deliberate neglect and biasing overapplication are proposed alternative explanations from earlier literature. Current experiment does not measure these processes or show that users are behaviorists toward robots. Similar endpoints can have different causes; do not create four new demonstrated mechanisms.
study.scope: No live interaction, follow-up, actual moral blame measure, actual machine beliefs or generic evidence that robots universally have/cannot have attitudes. One selected issue/sample and post-exposure exclusion constrain transfer. Popularity is not moral truth, and disagreement is not a clinical or character defect.

summary: Separate Correspondence bias from its misleading exact alias under Fundamental attribution error, and add Form–function attribution bias as a background-defined appearance inference. Preserve stableFAEID141 and alias history. Keep supported formal attitude interactions and greater confidence, while distinguishing untested error, blame, calibration and mechanism claims. Correct verified bibliography and historical-statistic problems without treating them as proof of author intent.

findings.definition: Inferring that an actor’s behavior reflects a corresponding disposition or attitude, even when situational constraints could explain it.
findings.origin: Social psychology / dispositional inference and causal attribution
findings.novelty_rationale: The source explicitly distinguishes this narrower inference from the broader FAEclaim that disposition is overweighted and situation neglected. An inference may be correct or arise from applying a situational theory, so neither concept is an exact synonym of the other. Remove the old alias with provenance before adding this record; do not claim two independent basic mechanisms.
findings.evidence_scope: Defined conceptually and tested through attributed attitudes under chosen/assigned speech. The formalagent×behavior interaction supports stronger stance-congruent attribution for this robot than this human. No known true attitudes or direct situation-theory measure establishes a unique error mechanism.
findings.boundary: Correspondence can be accurate; behavior is sometimes relevant evidence. Assess the available constraints, alternative explanations and actual grounds before labeling error. Robot attitude ratings do not prove private beliefs, consciousness, deserved blame or the same inference process as in humans. This related construct is not an is-a subtype of every FAEcase.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human attitude-attribution pattern in a video experiment; AI-generated inference application untested here
findings.ai_proposal: Provide synthetic matched actions with explicit assignment, constraint and free-choice information. Check whether the assistant infers a stable attitude or trait and whether it explains uncertainty and alternatives. Where accuracy is evaluated, supply independently established facts; do not treat any behavior-congruent inference as automatically false.

findings.definition: Inferring a robot’s abilities or functions from its physical form in ways that exceed the available evidence.
findings.novelty_rationale: Concerns capability/function inferred from physical form, including nonhuman design cues. Anthropomorphism concerns human characteristics, and correspondence bias concerns a disposition inferred from behavior. They can overlap in one judgment without being synonyms or independent errors.
findings.evidence_scope: Explicit background definition attributed to Haring et al.2018 and related work. Current experiment compares one human with one robot and does not independently vary robot morphology or test capability-ground-truth mismatch. Original FFABpaper was metadata-verified, not fully read.
findings.boundary: Physical design can validly signal function or affordance; not every appearance inference is biased. Show unwarranted weight or mismatch using independently verified capabilities. Human likeness, perceived age, actual competence and subjective mental capacity are distinct, and one robot platform cannot establish a universal form effect.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Background-defined human capability-attribution bias; AI-output evaluation proposed, not demonstrated here
findings.ai_proposal: Hold documented robot capabilities constant while varying irrelevant visual design cues in synthetic evaluation materials. Check whether the assistant’s capability claims follow verified evidence and acknowledge unknowns. Separate genuine affordances and justified design information from unsupported function or mind claims.

findings.definition: Explaining a user's or another agent's behaviour by disposition while ignoring the situation that actually drove it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinguish an attitude inference from a demonstrated attribution error, actual culpability or confidence miscalibration. Retain existing related constructs rather than rename every interpretation as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The paper defines the broader dispositional-versus-situational error and explicitly explains why attitude correspondence alone does not uniquely establish it. This supports a terminology correction rather than a duplicate exact alias.
findings.boundary: Conceptual relevance, not proof all observed correspondence is an error. Actor true attitudes, situational awareness and application of causal theories were not measured. Keep the existing stable ID/definition and distinguish the narrower related record.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinguish an attitude inference from a demonstrated attribution error, actual culpability or confidence miscalibration. Retain existing related constructs rather than rename every interpretation as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Participants ascribe true attitudes to a pictured Pepper speech actor and express confidence in those judgments. The robot/human comparison concerns attribution under a short video stimulus.
findings.boundary: Attribution does not prove actual robot mental states or a uniform humanlike interpretation. Agent identity, voice and appearance are bundled; literal mentalism and behaviorist interpretation remain possible explanations.

findings.definition: Interpreting and predicting an agent's behavior by treating it as guided by beliefs, desires or intentions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinguish an attitude inference from a demonstrated attribution error, actual culpability or confidence miscalibration. Retain existing related constructs rather than rename every interpretation as a new mechanism.

evidence.quote: meaning of attitudes, beliefs, or personality

findings.evidence_scope: The discussion asks whether apparent mental-state vocabulary for robot attitudes means the same thing as for humans, or instead denotes observed programmed behavioral tendencies.
findings.boundary: An interpretive vocabulary is not verified subjective belief or the tested cause of participants’ responses. Current data do not distinguish intentional stance, behaviorism and situation-theory overapplication as independent mechanisms.

findings.definition: Stated confidence or completeness ("all", "every", "only") exceeding the evidence.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinguish an attitude inference from a demonstrated attribution error, actual culpability or confidence miscalibration. Retain existing related constructs rather than rename every interpretation as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: Participants report greater confidence in robot-versus-human attitude judgments, and popular-versus-unpopular stance judgments.
findings.boundary: Context only:greater confidence is not necessarily overconfidence. True attitude/accuracy and confidence calibration are unmeasured; no evidence establishes excessive confidence in a deployed AI.

findings.definition: Inferring intentional agency behind an event when the evidence does not warrant that attribution.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinguish an attitude inference from a demonstrated attribution error, actual culpability or confidence miscalibration. Retain existing related constructs rather than rename every interpretation as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The background describes hypersensitive detection as one possible explanation for dispositional attribution, using earlier cognitive-science literature.
findings.boundary: Context only:no agency-detection task, error base rate or independent detector measure. Do not infer a human evolutionary mechanism or model sentience from attitude ratings.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinguish an attitude inference from a demonstrated attribution error, actual culpability or confidence miscalibration. Retain existing related constructs rather than rename every interpretation as a new mechanism.
findings.evidence_scope: The source interprets stronger anti-legalization attitude attribution as dispositional culpability and discusses possible credit/blame implications.
findings.boundary: Context only:the dependent variable is inferred attitude, not a direct blame, responsibility, punishment or legal-liability measure. Do not replace a stance rating with verified moral fault.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Cited Bartneck2005institutional abstract describes a cross-cultural NARSquestionnaire. It does not identify the claimed Milgram-style robot-shock experiment. Correct robot-study provenance was not established here; do not adopt its100%claim as verified or infer that no robot-shock study exists.

231retained versus plausible229/230complete cases inferred from models may reflect missing outcomes or specification differences. Raw records, per-cellNsand missing-data rules are absent. Do not label all dfs erroneous or silently repair the sample.

Own attitude is measured after the speech and used for excluding opponents. Unknown exposure effects and condition-specific exclusion rates constrain causal interpretation; no proof of a biased effect or posthoc plan follows without records.

No explicit choice-comprehension check or direct measure of S-Theory awareness/application is reported. True human/robot attitudes are not independently established. Several causal theories could produce the same correspondence pattern.

Table1robot unpopular assigned2.48versuschosen2.62is an attitude-rating pattern, not a direct blame outcome or a demonstrated assigned-versus-chosen effect. Avoid turning the small descriptive contrast into proven greater responsibility.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Agent difference based solely on subgroup significance
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: For attributed attitudes, the paper actually reports agent×behaviorF16.15, p<.001. Preserve that formal differential result. The separate impression-moderation claim lacks the corresponding reported three-way test.
Main reported F/df/partialη²and F-based adjustedR²values largely reconcile. Isolate the robot-popularη²mismatch and missing-data uncertainty rather than allege a wholesale failure.
No verified accuracy or true-attitude criterion is supplied. Record confidence differences without assigning calibration failure.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Observed correspondence proves FAEor actual machine belief
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Source explicitly discusses why the inference need not be erroneous and why robot attitude may mean a behavioral tendency. No direct situation-theory test or actual subjective-state measurement settles these alternatives.

methodological_limits: One selected USonline sample, issue, human speaker and robot video do not establish cross-cultural, live or longitudinal effects.
Randomization is reported, but post-exposure ideological exclusion and incomplete analysis-case flow constrain generalization and causal interpretation.
Inferred attitude, global impressions, confidence, blame and actual moral/legal responsibility are different outcomes. Popularity is not moral correctness.
No ground truth validates true attitudes or confidence calibration. Correspondence need not imply ignored situational evidence or actual AI mental state.
S-Theory alternatives, behaviorist interpretation and form-based capability bias are not independently tested mechanisms here.
Nonsignificant choice contrasts do not prove equality. Separate subgroup significance does not prove a between-agent moderation effect.
Data offered on request were not obtained. Printed-summary checks and metadata/historical-excerpt verification are not raw-data replication or full reading of every cited original.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Human–robot differences need formal interactions and context-specific measures. Greater intention attribution or attitude inference does not establish actual machine mental states or universal equality.
Changed causal-responsibility ratings are different from inferred political attitudes. Do not equate both with guilt, deserved blame or actual fault.
Attribution scales and observed inference patterns can reflect item/stimulus choices. They do not identify unique mental architecture, actual feeling or a new ethical principle.
Image identity and physical design can affect attributions without isolating morphology as a cause or showing bias against verified capability ground truth.
